name: United Kingdom
nativeName: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
traditionNote: Statute is supreme but incomplete on its own: decided cases bind later courts, so finding the law usually means reading an Act on legislation.gov.uk and then checking how the courts have interpreted it on Find Case Law.
summary: The UK Parliament at Westminster is legally sovereign and makes Acts of Parliament for the whole UK; the Scottish Parliament, Senedd Cymru and the Northern Ireland Assembly make their own Acts within devolved competence, and ministers make secondary legislation (statutory instruments, Scottish and Welsh statutory instruments, Northern Ireland statutory rules). Once a Bill receives Royal Assent it is published under the authority of the King's Printer on legislation.gov.uk, which is the official place of publication for newly enacted legislation and aims to publish within 24 hours. The Gazette (London, Edinburgh and Belfast editions) remains the official journal of record for statutory notices, proclamations, honours, insolvency and similar public acts, and has run since 1665. An Act does not necessarily take effect on Royal Assent: commencement is set by the Act itself or by a separate commencement order, and legislation.gov.uk records commencement information alongside the text. The authentic text is the King's Printer text as enacted or as made; the revised, consolidated version on the same site is editorially maintained and carries warnings where amendments have not yet been applied.
hierarchy: Acts of the UK Parliament (parliamentary sovereignty)
Acts of the Scottish Parliament, Acts of Senedd Cymru and Acts of the Northern Ireland Assembly, within devolved competence
Statutory instruments, Scottish and Welsh statutory instruments, and Northern Ireland statutory rules
Assimilated law (formerly retained EU law), as modified by the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023
Common law and binding judicial precedent
Constitutional conventions (binding in practice, not enforced by the courts)

gazette.name: The Gazette (London, Edinburgh and Belfast)
gazette.authority: His Majesty's Stationery Office (HMSO), The National Archives; published by TSO for the King's Printer
gazette.coverage: 1665-present; London edition every working day, Edinburgh edition twice weekly (Monday and Wednesday), Belfast edition weekly (from 1921), plus a combined Daily Edition covering all three
gazette.desc: The UK's official public record and journal of record: statutory notices, royal proclamations, honours and appointments, insolvency and bankruptcy, wills and probate, planning and company notices. There are over 450 notice types, of which several hundred are required by law to be published here. It is where publication in the Gazette is itself a legal requirement, not where Acts of Parliament are published.
gazette.howto: Go to Notices then All notices from the main navigation. You can search by free text, notice type, notice code, location, date or edition, and there are dedicated entry points for insolvency, wills and probate, awards and honours, and company information. Note that notice type, notice code and location searches only work on notices published from 1998 onwards. Every notice has a permanent notice ID and a PDF of the printed page it appeared in.
gazette.note: Searching and reading is free; a free account (MyGazette) is only needed to save searches or build bespoke editions.

constitution.name: The Cabinet Manual
constitution.coverage: First edition published 14 December 2010; not systematically revised since
constitution.desc: The UK has no codified constitution, so there is no single document to link. This is the closest official substitute: a Cabinet Office guide to the laws, rules and conventions governing the operation of government, covering the monarchy, elections and government formation, Cabinet, ministers, the civil service and the devolved administrations. The constitution itself is spread across statutes of constitutional significance (Magna Carta 1297, the Bill of Rights 1689, the Acts of Union, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the Human Rights Act 1998, the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 and the devolution Acts), common law, the royal prerogative and unwritten convention.
constitution.howto: Download the Cabinet Manual PDF from the publication page for the conventions; for the constitutional statutes themselves, look each one up by name on legislation.gov.uk, which holds all of them in revised form.
constitution.note: The Cabinet Manual is a description of practice, not law, and is not enforceable; it has not been comprehensively updated since 2011.

sources.name: legislation.gov.uk
sources.authority: The National Archives, on behalf of HM Government; published under the authority of the King's Printer
sources.coverage: Oldest item is from 1267, but coverage is only near-complete for legislation published from 1988 onwards; revised texts generally start from the 1 February 1991 base date. All UK Statutory Instruments from 1987, patchy before that. The site itself describes its holdings as a partial dataset of over 300,000 items.
sources.desc: The single official home of UK legislation and the official place of publication for newly enacted law. It holds every item in two forms: the as-enacted or as-made King's Printer text, and a revised consolidated text maintained by the editorial team at The National Archives and the Northern Ireland Statutory Publications Office. It also covers the devolved legislatures, Church Measures and Northern Ireland Orders in Council, and is available in Welsh as well as English.
sources.howto: Use the homepage Search Legislation form, which takes title or title keywords plus optional year, number and type, or open Advanced Search for full-text searching. You can also go straight to a URL of the form legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15 for the Equality Act 2010. On an item, Explore our collections and the Changes over time timeline let you move between the current revised text, the text as at an earlier date, and the original as-enacted or as-made version.
sources.note: Revised text can lag. A Changes to legislation status box at the top of each item states whether it is up to date as at a given date and, where effects have been recorded but not yet written into the text, offers a View outstanding changes link. The site reports over 95% of primary legislation as up to date.

sources.name: Changes to Legislation
sources.coverage: Effects on UK primary legislation made by legislation enacted from 2002 onwards; effects made by secondary legislation from 1971 onwards. Pre-2002 changes are already incorporated in the revised text and are not listed separately.
sources.desc: The amendment ledger behind the revised texts. It lists repeals, amendments, modifications and commencement effects recorded by the editorial team, including the crucial set of effects that have been identified but not yet applied to the consolidated text. This is how you tell whether the version you are reading is actually current.
sources.howto: Search by affected legislation (the Act you are reading) or by affecting legislation (the amending instrument), filtered by year and type. Results show each effect, the provision it hits, the instrument that made it, and whether it has been applied yet.
sources.note: Most new effects appear within about two weeks of publication, but large or high-volume instruments can take up to six weeks to be analysed.

sources.name: UK Statutory Instruments
sources.desc: The browse path for UK-wide secondary legislation, where most operative detail actually lives: regulations, orders, rules and commencement orders made by ministers under powers in Acts. Parallel paths exist for Scottish Statutory Instruments (ssi), Welsh Statutory Instruments (wsi) and Northern Ireland Statutory Rules (nisr).
sources.howto: Browse by year and number, or cite directly as legislation.gov.uk/uksi/YEAR/NUMBER (for example uksi/2024/1155 for The Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024). Add /made for the original text and /contents for the current version; most instruments also carry an Explanatory Memorandum PDF.
sources.note: An SI is often made months before it comes into force; check the commencement provision at the front of the instrument rather than assuming the made date.

sources.name: EU legislation and UK law
sources.coverage: EU instruments that applied in the UK before 11pm on 31 December 2020, as retained and subsequently amended
sources.desc: Explains and gives access to assimilated law: the body of EU-derived rules kept in force by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and renamed by the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023. Directly applicable EU regulations that survived Brexit are held on legislation.gov.uk as domestic instruments and are amended by UK statutory instruments.
sources.howto: Start here to work out whether an EU-origin rule was retained, revoked or replaced, then follow the links into the individual instrument on legislation.gov.uk and check its Changes to Legislation entry for the UK amendments made since 2021.
sources.note: The EUR-Lex text of the same instrument is the EU version and is not the law in force in the UK; only the legislation.gov.uk version reflects UK amendments.

sources.name: legislation.gov.uk data reuse documentation
sources.coverage: Whole of legislation.gov.uk, including revised text, as-enacted text, tables of contents, search feeds and change effects
sources.desc: The developer entry point for bulk and programmatic access, maintained by The National Archives. Any legislation URL returns machine-readable data by appending /data.xml for the marked-up text or /data.feed for Atom results on searches and lists; the underlying XML is Crown Legislation Markup Language (CLML), with an Akoma Ntoso representation also available, and there is a SPARQL endpoint for the linked-data model.
sources.howto: Read the API overview, then append /data.feed to any search or browse URL to get paginated Atom results (add results-count=N to change page size), or /data.xml to any item URL for the full marked-up text; /contents/data.xml and /section/N/data.xml work the same way for a table of contents or a single section.
sources.note: No API key, but requests must send a user agent and each IP is limited to 3,000 requests per five minutes; content is Crown copyright under the Open Government Licence.

sources.name: Parliamentary Bills
sources.authority: UK Parliament (House of Commons and House of Lords)
sources.coverage: All Bills from the 2006-07 session onwards; earlier Bills via the parliament.uk previous sessions pages
sources.desc: Where a law lives before it is a law. Tracks every Public, Private and Hybrid Bill through first reading, second reading, committee, report, third reading, Lords stages, ping-pong and Royal Assent, with the text of the Bill as introduced and as amended at each stage, plus explanatory notes, amendment papers and impact assessments.
sources.howto: Use Find a Bill to search by title or filter by session and current stage; each Bill page carries a stage-by-stage timeline with the dated publications attached to each stage. Once a Bill receives Royal Assent the page links out to the Act on legislation.gov.uk. RSS feeds are offered for all Bills, Public Bills and Private Bills.
sources.note: Bill text is superseded the moment it is amended, and a Bill is not law in force at any stage of its passage.

sources.name: Hansard
sources.coverage: 1803-present, Commons and Lords; the historic 1803-2005 archive is served alongside the modern record
sources.desc: The Official Report of debates in both Houses, and the standard source for the parliamentary context of a provision: what a minister said a clause was for, what amendments were resisted and why. The site states that daily debates are published the next working day.
sources.howto: Use Find in Hansard to search by keyword, member, date or debate title, and filter by House and by type (debate, written statement, written question); there is also a Find by volume/column number lookup for citing older material. Bill stage debates can also be reached from the corresponding stage on the Bills site.
sources.note: Hansard was selective before it became the Official Report in 1909; earlier coverage is not a complete record of everything said.

sources.name: The Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
sources.authority: The Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
sources.coverage: October 2009 to present; appeals decided before 31 July 2009 were House of Lords decisions and are held elsewhere
sources.desc: The final court of appeal for civil cases from the whole UK and for criminal cases from England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and the court that decides devolution issues. Case pages carry a case summary, the judgment and press summary, archived hearing video, the parties' written cases and the statement of facts and issues, plus the previous proceedings and a change log.
sources.howto: Search the case list using exact terms, party names or phrases, or filter by case status (for example Permission to Appeal application lodged, Awaiting hearing date, Judgment promulgated), area of law, date of issue, hearing date or judgment date, and sort by any of those dates. Case URLs take the form supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-YYYY-NNNN.
sources.note: Judgments and press summaries are now published here in both PDF and HTML; Find Case Law and BAILII carry the same judgments under their own citations.

sources.name: Find Case Law
sources.coverage: Courts and tribunals of England and Wales plus the UK Supreme Court and Judicial Committee of the Privy Council; most series begin in the early 2000s, the Supreme Court from 2009
sources.desc: The official archive of court judgments and tribunal decisions, and the place judgments are now deposited by the courts themselves. It is the authoritative free source for a judgment in HTML and PDF, identified by neutral citation.
sources.howto: Search by neutral citation ([2024] UKSC 12), party name or free text, or browse by court and tribunal; advanced search adds date, judge and court filters. Every judgment has a stable URL derived from its neutral citation.
sources.note: Reading and ordinary re-use are free under the Open Justice Licence, but bulk or computational analysis across the corpus requires a free licence application.

sources.name: Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service - Judgments
sources.coverage: Judgments from 1999 onwards, across the Court of Session, the High Court of Justiciary, the Sheriff Appeal Court and the Sheriff Courts
sources.desc: Scotland has its own legal system and its own courts, and Scottish judgments are not on Find Case Law. This is the official source for opinions of the Court of Session, the High Court of Justiciary, the Sheriff Appeal Court and the Sheriff Courts.
sources.howto: Follow the judgments section through to the search, which takes a keyword and filters by court and by date published, covering 1999 onwards. Sentencing statements, summaries of court opinions and the findings of fatal accident inquiries are published separately on the Judiciary of Scotland site at judiciary.scot.
sources.note: Many Scottish decisions are given orally and never reduced to writing, so the database is not a complete record of what the courts have decided.

sources.name: Judiciary NI - Judicial decisions and directions
sources.authority: Lord Chief Justice's Office, Northern Ireland
sources.coverage: Decisions dated from 1968 to the present: around 6,600 judgments plus practice directions and decisions of the Lands, Care and Charity Tribunals
sources.desc: The official source for judgments of the Court of Appeal, High Court, Crown Court and county courts in Northern Ireland, which forms a third legal jurisdiction distinct from England and Wales and from Scotland. It also carries practice directions and Northern Ireland tribunal decisions.
sources.howto: Use the decisions search and apply the filters for type of decision (judgment, practice direction, or a named tribunal), judicial officer, and year. If the judgment you need is not online, the Lord Chief Justice's Office library will try to source it on request at Library@judiciaryni.uk.

sources.name: British and Irish Legal Information Institute (BAILII)
sources.authority: BAILII, a registered charity, hosted by the Institute of Advanced Legal Studies (London) and University College Cork
sources.coverage: Over 240,000 decisions, mostly 1996 to present, plus selected older material; England and Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Ireland, the Channel Islands, the CJEU and the ECtHR
sources.desc: Not an official publisher, but for decades the only free full-text archive spanning all three UK jurisdictions plus Ireland and the European courts, and still the practical first stop for older or Scottish and Northern Irish judgments that Find Case Law does not carry. It also mirrors legislation and some law reform materials.
sources.howto: Use the case-law search across databases, or browse by jurisdiction then court then year; citation search accepts neutral citations and traditional report citations.
sources.note: BAILII is a charity, not an official publisher, and its texts are transcriptions rather than the official version for any jurisdiction. The site now sits behind an anti-bot interstitial, so it may take a moment to load and is not reliably reachable by scripts.

sources.name: Scottish Parliament - Bills and Laws
sources.coverage: Bills of the current and previous sessions since devolution in 1999
sources.desc: Where Acts of the Scottish Parliament (cited asp) begin. Covers Government, Members', Committee, Private and Hybrid Bills through their stage 1, 2 and 3 process, with the Bill as introduced, amendments, committee reports and policy memoranda.
sources.howto: Browse current Bills or search previous Bills by title and session; each Bill page carries its documents by stage and, once passed and given Royal Assent, links to the Act on legislation.gov.uk.
sources.note: The enacted text of an Act of the Scottish Parliament is published on legislation.gov.uk, not here.

sources.name: Senedd Cymru - Legislation
sources.coverage: Public Bills of the current and previous Senedd terms, plus subordinate legislation laid before the Senedd
sources.desc: The legislative business hub for Wales: Public Bills introduced by the Welsh Government, a Senedd committee, an individual Member or the Senedd Commission, tracked through the four-stage scrutiny process, together with the guide to the legislative process and subordinate legislation laid before the Senedd.
sources.howto: Follow the legislation section to the Bill you want, or use the separate business.senedd.wales records system for the full documentary history of an item; every page is available in Welsh and English.
sources.note: Welsh law is published bilingually; the enacted text of Acts of Senedd Cymru appears on legislation.gov.uk in both Welsh and English.

sources.name: Northern Ireland Assembly - Legislation
sources.coverage: 1999 to present across the current and archived Assembly sites, organised by mandate
sources.desc: Bills before the Northern Ireland Assembly with their explanatory and financial memoranda, marshalled lists of amendments and stage-by-stage versions, plus the delegated legislation stream and the Examiner of Statutory Rules reports on statutory rules laid before the Assembly.
sources.howto: Pick the mandate (for example 2022-2027) and then Primary Legislation - Bills to open a Bill and its documents; older material from earlier mandates sits on the archive site linked from the same section.
sources.note: The Assembly has been suspended for long stretches, during which Northern Ireland legislation was made at Westminster by Order in Council; those instruments are on legislation.gov.uk, not here.

sources.name: Law Wales
sources.coverage: Welsh law and the constitution of Wales, organised into three subject hubs: Culture, Environment and Public services
sources.desc: The Welsh Government's official explanatory guide to what law applies in Wales and who made it, with an overview of Welsh law plus commentary on housing, transport, planning, health and social care, and on the constitution of Wales. Useful because devolution boundaries make it genuinely hard to tell which of two parallel regimes applies in Wales. Content is published under the Open Government Licence and includes signed articles by outside contributors.
sources.howto: Pick one of the three subject hubs (Culture, Environment or Public services) to reach the commentary for an area and find out which body legislates in it, then follow the links to the instruments themselves on legislation.gov.uk.
sources.note: Commentary only, published in English and expressly not legal advice; it is not the legislative text and can lag behind changes. Despite the subject matter the site has no Welsh-language version, unlike legislation.gov.uk and senedd.wales.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of an Act of Parliament
findLaw.steps: Search the Act's short title and year in the Search Legislation form on legislation.gov.uk, then open its table of contents. Read the Changes to legislation box at the top: it states the date the text is up to date to, and where effects have been recorded but not yet applied it offers a View outstanding changes link. Use the Changes over time timeline to read the text as it stood at an earlier date or as originally enacted.

findLaw.task: See what has changed, and what has not yet been applied
findLaw.steps: Open the Changes to Legislation search and query by affected legislation (the Act you are reading) or by affecting legislation (the amending instrument). The result list shows each repeal, amendment, modification or commencement, the instrument that made it, and whether the editorial team has applied it yet.

Search Find Case Law by neutral citation, party name or keyword; it holds England and Wales courts and tribunals plus the UK Supreme Court and Privy Council. For Scottish judgments use the Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service database, and for Northern Ireland use Judiciary NI.
findLaw.source: Find Case Law, The National Archives

findLaw.task: Find a regulation, order or commencement instrument
findLaw.steps: Browse UK Statutory Instruments by year and number on legislation.gov.uk, or go directly to legislation.gov.uk/uksi/YEAR/NUMBER. Swap uksi for ssi, wsi or nisr for Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland instruments, and read the Explanatory Memorandum PDF attached to the instrument for plain-language context.

findLaw.task: Find law made by a devolved legislature
findLaw.steps: On legislation.gov.uk use Browse Legislation and pick the type: Acts of the Scottish Parliament (asp), Acts of Senedd Cymru and earlier Welsh Acts and Measures (asc, anaw, mwa), or Acts of the Northern Ireland Assembly (nia). For a measure still in progress, go instead to the relevant legislature's own Bills pages.

findLaw.task: Track a Bill that has not yet become law
findLaw.steps: Search bills.parliament.uk by title and open the Bill page, which shows the stage timeline in both Houses and attaches the text as introduced, amendment papers, explanatory notes and impact assessments to each stage. After Royal Assent the page links to the Act on legislation.gov.uk.

findLaw.task: Find an official statutory notice (insolvency, probate, honours, planning)
findLaw.steps: Open Notices then All notices on The Gazette and search by free text, notice type, notice code, location, date or edition; notice type, notice code and location filters only apply to notices published from 1998 onwards. Each notice has a permanent ID and a PDF of the printed Gazette page it appeared in, which is the citable record.

subnational: The UK is a union of four countries with three separate legal systems - England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland - and three devolved legislatures that make primary law within their competence: the Scottish Parliament, Senedd Cymru and the Northern Ireland Assembly. Their Acts and statutory instruments are all published on legislation.gov.uk alongside Westminster legislation, distinguished by type code (asp, asc/anaw, nia, ssi, wsi, nisr); the legislatures' own sites carry the Bills and the scrutiny record. Below that level, local authorities make byelaws, which are confirmed by the relevant minister and are generally published by the authority itself rather than centrally, so there is no single national index of them. The Crown Dependencies (Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man) and the British Overseas Territories are not part of the UK and have their own legislatures and their own publication sites.
caveats: Only the King's Printer text as enacted or as made is the authoritative version; the revised consolidated text on legislation.gov.uk is an editorial product, and its own Changes to legislation status box flags where recorded amendments have not yet been applied, with a backlog of weeks or longer in busy periods and thinner revision coverage for older Scottish and Northern Ireland material. The Gazette is the official journal of record for notices but is not where Acts are published, and legislation.gov.uk is not a gazette in the continental sense - two different official channels answer two different questions. Find Case Law is the official judgment archive but only reaches back to roughly the early 2000s for most courts, does not cover Scotland or Northern Ireland, and captures only judgments that were written down; a great deal of first-instance decision-making is oral and simply does not exist as a document. BAILII, ICLR, Westlaw and LexisNexis are private or charitable publishers, not official ones, and the traditional Law Reports that courts prefer to be cited from are behind paywalls even though the underlying judgments are free. Explanatory notes, explanatory memoranda, the Cabinet Manual and guidance published on gov.uk are aids to understanding and carry no legal force, and Bill text ceases to reflect anything the moment the Bill is amended.
